prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

HARARE, Zimbabwe (CNN) -- Some of Zimbabwe's children are "wasting away" as political turmoil and economic crisis have caused a severe food shortage, according to a report from Save the Children. Children sleep in rough conditions on the border between Zimbabwe and South Africa. The number of acute child malnutrition cases has risen by almost two-thirds in the past year, the report from the UK-based agency said in its appeal to world donors for help. "There is no excuse for failing to provide this food," program director Lynn Walker said. "The innocent people of Zimbabwe should not be made to suffer for a political situation that is out of their control." Five million Zimbabweans -- out of a population of about 12 million -- are in need of food aid now, the report said. The group is appealing for 18,000 tons of food for next month. "We have already been forced to reduce the rations of emergency food we are delivering because there isn't enough to go around," the report said. "If, as we fear, the food aid pipeline into Zimbabwe begins to fail in the new year the millions of people who rely on emergency food aid will suffer." Zimbabwe is facing its worst economic and humanitarian crisis since its independence from Great Britain 28 years ago. There is an acute shortage of all essentials such as cash, fuel, medical drugs, electricity and food. President Robert Mugabe blames the crisis on the sanctions imposed on him and his cronies by the West for allegedly disregarding human rights. But Mugabe's critics attribute the crisis to his economic policies. As the economy has faltered for almost a decade now, a cholera epidemic is raging, fueled by the collapse of health, sanitation and water services in Zimbabwe. The epidemic has claimed more than 1,100 lives and infected more than 20,000 people since its outbreak in August. Health experts have warned that the water-borne disease could infect more than 60,000 unless its spread is halted. The political crisis rose to a boil in this year when the opposition party claimed that it won the presidential election, but Mugabe's government refused to recognize the result. Instead, the race was thrown to a runoff, which was boycotted by the opposition. Mugabe signed an agreement with the opposition in September to form a unity government, but a bitter dispute over the division of cabinet seats has prevented its formation. Inflation is so severe that the government was forced to print $10 billion currency notes last week, with each expected to buy just 20 loaves of bread.

HARARE, Zimbabwe (CNN) — A Save the Children report says Zimbabwe’s political unrest and economic collapse have created a grave food crisis, leaving some children “wasting away.”

Children are sleeping in harsh conditions along the border separating Zimbabwe from South Africa. In an appeal to international donors, the UK-based organization said cases of acute malnutrition among children have increased by nearly two-thirds over the last year.

“There is no excuse for failing to provide this food,” said Lynn Walker, the group’s program director. “The innocent people of Zimbabwe should not be made to suffer for a political situation that is out of their control.”

According to the report, 5 million Zimbabweans, from a total population of roughly 12 million, currently require food assistance. Save the Children is seeking 18,000 tons of food for the coming month.

“We have already been forced to reduce the rations of emergency food we are delivering because there isn’t enough to go around,” the report stated. “If, as we fear, the food aid pipeline into Zimbabwe begins to fail in the new year the millions of people who rely on emergency food aid will suffer.”

Zimbabwe is experiencing its most serious economic and humanitarian emergency since gaining independence from Britain 28 years ago. The country is suffering severe shortages of basic necessities, including money, fuel, medicines, electricity and food.

President Robert Mugabe has blamed the crisis on Western sanctions imposed on him and his allies over alleged human rights abuses. His opponents, however, say his economic decisions are responsible.

After nearly a decade of economic decline, Zimbabwe is also battling a cholera outbreak, worsened by the breakdown of health care, sanitation and water systems. Since the disease emerged in August, it has killed more than 1,100 people and infected over 20,000. Medical specialists have cautioned that, unless the outbreak is contained, more than 60,000 people could contract the waterborne illness.

The country’s political crisis intensified this year after the opposition said it had won the presidential election, while Mugabe’s government rejected that claim. The vote was then sent to a runoff, which the opposition boycotted.

In September, Mugabe reached a deal with the opposition to create a unity government, but the arrangement has not been implemented because of a fierce disagreement over how cabinet positions should be allocated.

Inflation has become so extreme that the government had to issue $10 billion banknotes last week, each of which was expected to purchase only about 20 loaves of bread.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news article about Zimbabwe’s humanitarian crisis, focusing on Save the Children’s warning about rising child malnutrition and food shortages.
counterfactuals.output:
**Save the Children warns Zimbabwe’s food crisis is pushing more children into malnutrition**

**Harare, Zimbabwe** — A worsening hunger crisis in Zimbabwe is putting growing numbers of children at risk of acute malnutrition, Save the Children has warned, as food shortages deepen across the country following poor harvests and prolonged dry conditions.

The aid agency said families in some of the hardest-hit areas are running out of food months before the next harvest, forcing parents to cut meals, reduce portion sizes or rely on less nutritious foods. Children are among the most vulnerable, with aid workers warning that a lack of adequate food can quickly lead to wasting, stunted growth and increased risk of illness.

Zimbabwe has been grappling with severe food insecurity after drought conditions linked to the El Niño weather pattern damaged crops across southern Africa. Maize, the country’s staple food, has been particularly affected, leaving many rural households with little or no harvest to sustain them.

Save the Children said the crisis is being worsened by rising food prices, limited access to clean water in some communities and the strain on already fragile health services. The organization warned that without urgent support, more children could face life-threatening malnutrition in the coming months.

“Families are making impossible choices,” the agency said in its warning, describing households that are prioritizing survival over schooling, health care and other basic needs.

Humanitarian organizations say children who are malnourished are more likely to fall sick from preventable diseases, while prolonged hunger can also affect learning and development. In areas where food shortages are severe, some children may miss school as families search for work, food or water.

Zimbabwean authorities have previously appealed for assistance to respond to drought-related hunger, while aid groups have called for increased funding for food aid, nutrition programs, clean water, health care and support for farmers ahead of the next planting season.

The crisis in Zimbabwe is part of a broader emergency across southern Africa, where drought has left millions of people in need of food assistance. Relief agencies say the situation could deteriorate further if funding gaps persist and if families are unable to rebuild their livelihoods before the next harvest.

Save the Children urged donors and governments to act quickly, warning that delays in humanitarian response could have long-term consequences for Zimbabwe’s children.

“Malnutrition is not just about hunger today,” the agency said. “For children, it can shape the rest of their lives.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the situation in Zimbabwe during its political and economic crisis, including food aid shortages, cholera, inflation, and the Mugabe opposition dispute, in the style of an international news report.
counterfactuals.output:
Zimbabwe is facing a deepening political and economic crisis marked by food shortages, disease, hyperinflation and a bitter dispute over power between President Robert Mugabe and the opposition.

Aid agencies have warned that millions of Zimbabweans are in need of emergency food assistance, but relief efforts have been hampered by funding gaps, logistical problems and political tensions. The shortages come after years of economic decline, disrupted agricultural production and the collapse of basic services.

A major cholera outbreak has added to the emergency, spreading through communities where water and sanitation systems have broken down. Hospitals and clinics, already short of medicines, staff and equipment, have struggled to cope with the rising number of cases.

The economy has continued to deteriorate, with inflation reaching extreme levels and the local currency losing value at a staggering pace. Prices for basic goods have soared, wages have become almost meaningless, and many shops have either closed or switched to foreign currency transactions.

At the center of the crisis is the unresolved political confrontation between Mr. Mugabe and the opposition, led by Morgan Tsvangirai’s Movement for Democratic Change. Disputes over elections, violence, and the terms of a proposed power-sharing arrangement have delayed the formation of an effective government. The opposition has accused Mr. Mugabe’s ZANU-PF party of clinging to power and using state institutions against its rivals, while Mugabe’s supporters have blamed Western sanctions and foreign interference for the country’s collapse.

Regional leaders and international governments have urged both sides to reach an agreement, warning that continued deadlock is worsening the humanitarian emergency. For many Zimbabweans, however, the immediate concern remains survival: finding food, safe water, medicine and a stable means of living amid one of the country’s gravest crises since independence.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

HARARE, Zimbabwe — Save the Children has appealed for urgent emergency food assistance for children in Zimbabwe, warning that worsening malnutrition, economic distress and national instability are pushing many families to the brink.

The aid agency said children are increasingly at risk as households struggle with food shortages, rising prices and disruptions to basic services. It urged donors, humanitarian agencies and Zimbabwean authorities to scale up support for nutrition programs, school feeding, health services and cash assistance for vulnerable families.

“Children are bearing the heaviest burden of this crisis,” the organization said in an appeal, warning that without swift intervention, more children could suffer acute malnutrition, illness and interrupted education.

Zimbabwe has faced recurring food insecurity driven by drought, high inflation, unemployment and pressure on public services. In many communities, families have reduced the number of meals they eat each day, while some children are going to school hungry or dropping out to help support their households.

Health workers and aid groups have also expressed concern that malnutrition is weakening children’s immune systems, making them more vulnerable to disease. Shortages of clean water and strain on clinics have compounded the risks, particularly in rural areas and poorer urban neighborhoods.

Save the Children called for immediate funding to expand screening and treatment for malnourished children, provide supplementary feeding for infants and pregnant and breastfeeding women, and help families buy food before the situation deteriorates further.

The agency said long-term support is also needed to strengthen community resilience, including investment in agriculture, social protection and services for children affected by poverty and displacement.

Zimbabwean officials have acknowledged food security challenges and have previously appealed for support during periods of drought and economic hardship. Aid groups say the coming months will be critical in preventing a deeper humanitarian crisis.

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a detailed article on Zimbabwe’s late-2000s crisis, mentioning Robert Mugabe, sanctions, hyperinflation, cholera deaths, failed unity government talks, and millions needing food aid.
counterfactuals.output:
# Zimbabwe’s Late-2000s Crisis: Political Breakdown, Hyperinflation, Hunger, and Disease

In the late 2000s, Zimbabwe experienced one of the most severe political, economic, and humanitarian crises in modern African history. Under President Robert Mugabe and his ruling party, the Zimbabwe African National Union–Patriotic Front (ZANU-PF), the country was gripped by economic collapse, disputed elections, international isolation, mass food insecurity, and a deadly cholera outbreak. By 2008 and 2009, Zimbabwe had become a symbol of state failure: its currency was virtually worthless, hospitals and schools were barely functioning, millions needed food aid, and political negotiations intended to end the crisis repeatedly stalled.

## Political crisis under Robert Mugabe

Robert Mugabe had ruled Zimbabwe since independence in 1980, first as prime minister and later as president. Once praised as a liberation leader, he became increasingly authoritarian over time, especially after the emergence of a strong opposition movement, the Movement for Democratic Change (MDC), led by Morgan Tsvangirai.

The political crisis deepened dramatically after the 2008 elections. In the March 2008 vote, the MDC won a parliamentary majority, and Tsvangirai outpolled Mugabe in the presidential race, though official results said he had not secured enough votes to avoid a run-off. The period that followed was marked by violence and intimidation against opposition supporters. Tsvangirai withdrew from the June run-off, saying the election could not be free or fair amid attacks on MDC members and activists. Mugabe proceeded as the sole major candidate and claimed victory, but the election was widely condemned internationally.

Regional leaders, particularly through the Southern African Development Community (SADC), attempted to mediate between ZANU-PF and the MDC. A power-sharing agreement was announced in September 2008, intended to create a unity government with Mugabe as president and Tsvangirai as prime minister. However, talks over the distribution of key ministries—especially home affairs, which controlled the police—repeatedly failed or stalled. The failure of unity government negotiations prolonged uncertainty and deepened the suffering of ordinary Zimbabweans. Although a unity government was eventually formed in February 2009, the months of deadlock in late 2008 occurred during the height of the country’s economic and humanitarian collapse.

## Sanctions and international isolation

Zimbabwe’s government blamed much of the crisis on Western sanctions, especially those imposed by the United States, the European Union, and other countries. These measures targeted Mugabe, senior ZANU-PF officials, and associated entities, including travel bans and asset freezes. Western governments argued that sanctions were a response to human rights abuses, election violence, corruption, and the erosion of democratic institutions.

The impact and meaning of sanctions became heavily politicized. Mugabe and ZANU-PF described them as a form of economic warfare designed to remove the government. Critics of Mugabe argued that Zimbabwe’s collapse was primarily caused by domestic mismanagement, corruption, political repression, destructive land policies, and the undermining of property rights and investor confidence. In practice, Zimbabwe’s isolation from major donors and financial institutions made recovery harder, but the country’s internal governance failures were central to the depth of the crisis.

## Hyperinflation and economic collapse

The most visible sign of Zimbabwe’s collapse was hyperinflation. By 2008, prices were rising at a pace that made normal economic life impossible. Wages lost value within hours, shops changed prices multiple times a day, and people carried bags of banknotes to buy basic goods. The government printed increasingly large denominations, including notes in the billions and trillions of Zimbabwean dollars, but these became almost worthless almost immediately.

Official inflation figures became unreliable and were eventually abandoned, but estimates placed Zimbabwe’s inflation rate among the highest ever recorded. In late 2008, some economists estimated inflation in the billions or even higher on an annualized basis. Savings were wiped out, pensions became meaningless, and salaries could not cover transport to work, let alone food or medicine.

The roots of hyperinflation included the state’s heavy money printing to finance spending, collapsing production, shortages of foreign currency, and the broader breakdown of confidence in the economy. Agricultural output had fallen sharply after the fast-track land reform program that began in 2000, which redistributed land from white commercial farmers but often without sufficient planning, support, or secure financing for new farmers. Manufacturing also declined, and unemployment soared. By the end of the decade, many Zimbabweans survived through informal trading, remittances from relatives abroad, barter, or humanitarian assistance.

In 2009, the Zimbabwean dollar was effectively abandoned in favor of foreign currencies such as the U.S. dollar and the South African rand, which helped stabilize prices. But by then, the damage to livelihoods, institutions, and public trust was immense.

## Millions needing food aid

Food insecurity was one of the most devastating consequences of the crisis. Once considered a regional breadbasket, Zimbabwe became dependent on food imports and humanitarian relief. Poor harvests, disrupted agriculture, lack of inputs such as seed and fertilizer, economic mismanagement, and the inability of the state to maintain basic distribution systems all contributed to shortages.

By late 2008 and early 2009, the United Nations and humanitarian agencies estimated that millions of Zimbabweans needed food aid. Some estimates suggested that around five million people—nearly half the population—were in need of assistance at the height of the crisis. Many families reduced meals, sold possessions, pulled children out of school, or crossed borders into South Africa, Botswana, Mozambique, and Zambia in search of work or food.

Humanitarian agencies faced logistical difficulties, political restrictions, and funding constraints. Aid distribution was also politically sensitive, with accusations that food could be manipulated for partisan purposes. For ordinary Zimbabweans, the crisis meant hunger, malnutrition, and a daily struggle to find maize meal, cooking oil, clean water, and basic medicine.

## Cholera outbreak and thousands of deaths

As the economy collapsed, so did public infrastructure. Water treatment systems failed, sewage systems broke down, garbage collection stopped in many areas, and hospitals lacked staff, medicine, and functioning equipment. These conditions helped trigger a catastrophic cholera outbreak beginning in 2008.

Cholera spread rapidly through contaminated water, particularly in densely populated urban areas and communities with poor sanitation. The outbreak exposed the near-total breakdown of Zimbabwe’s public health system. Clinics and hospitals were overwhelmed, while many health workers had left the country or stopped reporting to work because their salaries were worthless.

By the time the outbreak was brought under control, more than 4,000 people had died, and roughly 100,000 suspected cases had been reported. The scale of cholera deaths shocked the region and the wider world because cholera is treatable and preventable when clean water, sanitation, and basic medical care are available. The epidemic became one of the clearest indicators of the depth of Zimbabwe’s state failure.

## Failed talks and delayed recovery

The political deadlock after the 2008 elections worsened every other part of the crisis. Negotiations for a unity government were meant to create a path toward stabilization, but talks repeatedly failed over control of the security services, ministries, provincial governorships, and the balance of power between Mugabe’s ZANU-PF and Tsvangirai’s MDC. Each delay undermined confidence and discouraged international donors from re-engaging fully.

Regional mediators, especially South Africa, pushed both sides to compromise. The eventual Government of National Unity, formed in February 2009, helped bring a measure of stability. Dollarization curbed hyperinflation, shops began to restock, and some public services gradually resumed. However, the unity government was fragile, mistrust remained high, and deeper political reforms were limited.

## Human consequences

Behind the statistics were millions of individual tragedies. Teachers, nurses, civil servants, and factory workers saw their incomes vanish. Parents struggled to feed children. Students dropped out of school. Hospitals turned away patients because they lacked medicine, clean water, or staff. Many Zimbabweans migrated, creating a large diaspora across southern Africa and beyond.

The crisis also damaged national institutions. Courts, media, electoral bodies, police structures, and public services were widely viewed as politicized or weakened. Trust in the state eroded, and economic recovery was slowed by uncertainty over property rights, rule of law, and future political stability.

## Conclusion

Zimbabwe’s late-2000s crisis was the result of a combination of authoritarian politics, economic mismanagement, contested land reform, institutional collapse, international isolation, and failed or delayed political compromise. Robert Mugabe’s government blamed sanctions and foreign interference, while critics pointed to repression, corruption, and policy failures as the main causes. Whatever the interpretation, the consequences were undeniable: hyperinflation destroyed the currency, cholera killed thousands, millions required food aid, and failed unity government talks prolonged a national emergency.

The period remains one of the starkest examples of how political breakdown can turn into economic and humanitarian catastrophe. Zimbabwe’s eventual stabilization after 2009 showed that recovery was possible, but the damage inflicted during the late-2000s crisis left deep scars on the country’s economy, institutions, and people.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a CNN breaking-news-style report describing how Zimbabwe’s economic collapse and political turmoil have led to severe hunger, reduced food rations, and children “wasting away.”
counterfactuals.output:
**Breaking News-Style Report — Not affiliated with CNN**

**ANCHOR:**  
Breaking tonight: Zimbabwe is facing a deepening humanitarian crisis as economic collapse and political turmoil push millions toward hunger. Aid groups warn that food shortages are worsening, rations are being cut, and children in some communities are showing signs of severe malnutrition — described by health workers as “wasting away.”

**REPORTER VOICEOVER:**  
Across Zimbabwe, families are struggling to survive amid soaring prices, unemployment, currency instability, and repeated disruptions to food supplies. Years of economic strain, combined with political uncertainty and climate shocks, have left many households unable to afford even basic staples like maize meal, cooking oil, and beans.

Humanitarian agencies say the pressure is especially devastating in rural areas, where failed harvests and limited access to markets have left families dependent on food assistance. But those aid deliveries are shrinking. Reduced funding and growing demand have forced relief organizations to cut rations — meaning families who were already eating too little are now receiving even less.

**FIELD REPORTER:**  
In some villages, parents say they are skipping meals so their children can eat. But even that is no longer enough. Clinics are reporting rising numbers of children with visible signs of malnutrition: thin arms, swollen bellies, fatigue, and stunted growth. Health workers warn that without urgent intervention, the youngest children are at the greatest risk.

**LOCAL MOTHER:**  
“We eat once a day if we are lucky. Sometimes the children sleep hungry. They are getting weaker.”

**REPORTER VOICEOVER:**  
Zimbabwe’s crisis has been building for years. Hyperinflation, shortages of foreign currency, declining public services, and contested politics have weakened the economy and eroded trust in institutions. At the same time, droughts and erratic rainfall have battered agriculture, leaving many small farmers with little or nothing to harvest.

The result is a dangerous spiral: food becomes more expensive, wages lose value, families sell livestock or possessions to buy meals, and children fall further behind nutritionally.

**AID WORKER:**  
“We are seeing families make impossible choices. They need food, clean water, medical care — and they need it now. When rations are reduced, children are the first to suffer.”

**ANCHOR:**  
International organizations are calling for urgent funding to expand food distributions, support nutrition clinics, and stabilize communities before the hunger crisis worsens. For many families in Zimbabwe, the question tonight is not what they will eat tomorrow — but whether they will eat at all.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
